cards.back: A graph that joins points with a line. It is used for data that changes continuously, such as temperature over time.
cards.say: line graph. A graph that joins points with a line. It is used for data that changes continuously, such as temperature over time.

cards.back: A chart that uses bars to compare separate categories, such as favourite fruits.
cards.say: bar chart. A chart that uses bars to compare separate categories, such as favourite fruits.

cards.back: One of the two lines on a graph with a scale. The x axis goes across and the y axis goes up.
cards.say: axis. One of the two lines on a graph with a scale. The x axis goes across and the y axis goes up.

cards.front: Which variable goes on the x axis?
cards.back: The independent variable, the one you change.
cards.say: Which variable goes on the x axis? The independent variable, the one you change.

cards.front: Which variable goes on the y axis?
cards.back: The dependent variable, the one you measure.
cards.say: Which variable goes on the y axis? The dependent variable, the one you measure.

cards.front: Why must a graph have labels and units on the axes?
cards.back: So that anyone can see what was measured and in which units.
cards.say: Why must a graph have labels and units on the axes? So that anyone can see what was measured and in which units.

cards.back: The numbers marked along an axis. They must be evenly spaced.
cards.say: scale. The numbers marked along an axis. They must be evenly spaced.

cards.front: How do you plot a point on a line graph?
cards.back: Find the value on the x axis, go up to the value on the y axis and mark a small cross.
cards.say: How do you plot a point on a line graph? Find the value on the x axis, go up to the value on the y axis and mark a small cross.

cards.back: A smooth line or straight line that passes through or near most points, showing the trend.
cards.say: line of best fit. A smooth line or straight line that passes through or near most points, showing the trend.

cards.back: A trend or regular link in data, such as "the longer the heating time, the higher the temperature".
cards.say: pattern. A trend or regular link in data, such as the longer the heating time, the higher the temperature.

cards.back: A point that does not fit the pattern. Check it and measure again if possible.
cards.say: anomalous result. A point that does not fit the pattern. Check it and measure again if possible.

cards.back: The general direction in which data changes.
cards.say: trend. The general direction in which data changes.

cards.front: What does a steep line on a graph show?
cards.back: A fast change in the measurement.
cards.say: What does a steep line on a graph show? A fast change in the measurement.

cards.front: What does a flat line on a graph show?
cards.back: No change in the measurement.
cards.say: What does a flat line on a graph show? No change in the measurement.

cards.back: To read a value between two plotted points.
cards.say: interpolate. To read a value between two plotted points.

cards.back: To extend a graph beyond the measured points to predict a value. It is less certain.
cards.say: extrapolate. To extend a graph beyond the measured points to predict a value. It is less certain.

cards.back: What your evidence shows. It must be backed up by your results and answer the question.
cards.say: conclusion. What your evidence shows. It must be backed up by your results and answer the question.

cards.front: When does evidence support a conclusion?
cards.back: When the results clearly show the pattern and were repeated.
cards.say: When does evidence support a conclusion? When the results clearly show the pattern and were repeated.

cards.front: Why is one result not good evidence?
cards.back: It may be a mistake or luck. Repeated results are more reliable.
cards.say: Why is one result not good evidence? It may be a mistake or luck. Repeated results are more reliable.

cards.back: The sum of the values divided by how many there are. For 4, 6 and 8 the mean is 6.
cards.say: mean, in data. The sum of the values divided by how many there are. For four, six and eight, the mean is six.

cards.back: The difference between the largest and smallest values.
cards.say: range. The difference between the largest and smallest values.

cards.front: What is the range of 3, 7 and 12?
cards.back: Nine. Twelve minus three is nine.
cards.say: What is the range of 3, 7 and 12? Nine. Twelve minus three is nine.

cards.front: How can you improve the reliability of an investigation?
cards.back: Repeat the measurements, keep the control variables the same and take the mean of the results.
cards.say: How can you improve the reliability of an investigation? Repeat the measurements, keep the control variables the same and take the mean of the results.
